construction.access_recipe: Download the annual ZIPs f8612013.zip through f8612024.zip (and f8612025.zip for the final holdout labels) from the URLs above with plain HTTPS, no login, one file per year. Unzip each; open the Reliability workbook in that year's archive (sheet/file names follow the pattern Reliability_<year>, with .xls rather than .xlsx in some early vintages). Read the header with two header rows and match columns by text pattern rather than exact string, because the index columns appear in an IEEE-standard block and an other-standard block and EIA renamed the index columns at least once (third-party reusers report a 2021 relabelling): locate the utility number, utility name, state, ownership/standard indicator, customer or meter count, and the SAIDI/SAIFI/CAIDI columns carrying 'with MED'/'major event' and 'without MED'/'without major event' variants; drop trailing footnote rows. Normalise to one row per utility-year (drop utilities with more than one state row in a year), cast EIA dot placeholders to missing rather than zero, and build the wide panel keyed on utility number with years Y-3..Y+1. Compute the median baseline over Y-3..Y-1, form the target from CY Y+1 only, then cut the three splits at the frozen boundaries. Validate before labelling by customer-weighting the CY 2024 SAIDI columns to state and national totals and comparing against EIA's published Table 11.2 (2024 U.S. total: 662.6 minutes with major event days, 131.6 minutes without).
construction.expected_size: Estimated: 13 annual ZIPs, each a few megabytes to a few tens of megabytes, well under 1 GB total; the Reliability sheet is on the order of a thousand utility rows by a few dozen columns per year. After eligibility filters, roughly 4,000-7,000 utility-cohort rows and roughly 500-1,200 positive labels across the nine cohorts; both figures are estimates to be measured once the rules above are frozen, not tuned afterwards.
construction.format: Tabular CSV panel of utility-cohort rows (one row per EIA utility number per forecast year Y) with identifiers, the frozen binary target, and the frozen feature columns; emitted as train.csv, eval.csv and holdout.csv with an identical schema, plus a small manifest recording file vintages and row counts.
construction.source_examples: Documented checks a builder should reproduce: (1) the CY 2024 Reliability file must yield, after customer weighting, national SAIDI of about 662.6 minutes including major event days and 131.6 minutes excluding them, matching EIA Table 11.2 for 2024; (2) Florida's CY 2024 SAIDI including major event days is about 1,487.6 minutes versus 72.7 minutes for 2025, the hurricane-year contrast EIA publishes for that state; (3) utilities flagged as using a non-IEEE method must carry a reporting_standard value distinct from IEEE and be present in the other-standard column block; (4) every retained row must have four distinct annual values (Y-3, Y-2, Y-1, Y+1) with no interpolation.

evidence.claim: The Reliability schedule exists, is collected on Form EIA-861 from utilities, covers 2013 to present, and utilities may use IEEE standards or another method.
evidence.quote: The data contain information on non-momentary electrical interruptions. If collected, utilities report the system average interruption duration index (SAIDI), the system average interruption frequency index (SAIFI), and the conditions under which these metrics are collected.

evidence.claim: One ZIP per calendar year with stable file naming, including the 2024 and 2025 releases, is linked directly from the publisher page.
The 2025 release is labelled final data on the publisher page, so labels through CY 2025 exist.
EIA defines SAIDI, SAIFI and CAIDI and the major-event-day threshold in its own published reliability table.
evidence.quote: SAIDI = System Average Interruption Duration Index. It is the minutes of non-momentary electric interruptions, per year, the average customer experienced.

evidence.claim: Excluding major event days is a documented, published variant of the same metric, and MED identification differs by method.
evidence.quote: A Major Event Day is any day that exceeds a daily SAIDI threshold called Tmed.

evidence.claim: EIA publishes the aggregate reliability values we can use to validate a reconstructed utility-level panel.
evidence.quote: Table 11.2 Reliability Metrics Using IEEE of U.S. Distribution System by State, 2025 and 2024

evidence.claim: Utility-identifiable reliability responses are public information, supporting redistribution of the utility-level records.
evidence.quote: All other information reported on Form EIA-861 is considered public information and may be publicly released in company identifiable form.

evidence.claim: Reporting is mandatory under statute, so the annual files are a census-like frame rather than a voluntary convenience sample.
evidence.quote: This report is mandatory under Title 15 U.S.C. §772(b).

evidence.claim: EIA states its data and files are public domain, usable and redistributable, with an acknowledgment including a publication date.
evidence.quote: U.S. government publications are in the public domain and are not subject to copyright protection.

evidence.claim: Some material EIA hosts is third-party licensed, so upstream rights are not overwritten by the public-domain status of EIA data.
evidence.quote: You may see on our website documents, illustrations, photographs, or other information resources contributed or licensed by private individuals, companies, or organizations that may be protected by U.S. and foreign copyright laws.

limitations: Reliability indices are self-reported and unaudited by EIA; utilities may use IEEE 1366 or an internally defined method, and non-IEEE reporters self-determine which days are major event days, so the excluding-MED values are not strictly comparable across utilities.

Annual reliability is dominated by weather and storm occurrence, and the feature set deliberately contains no storm, outage-cause or capital-spending covariates, so a large share of label variance is unpredictable by construction; the task measures screening skill, not causal drivers.

This is a current-vintage retrospective built from today's published files: the values a regulator would have seen at the decision instant could differ from the final vintage, so no claim of proven historical operational availability is made.

Workbook layout is not stable across vintages: IEEE and other-standard column blocks coexist, some early files are .xls, and index columns were reportedly relabelled around 2021, so the parser must match headers by pattern and be re-checked for each new year.

The panel recurs utilities across cohorts; features are capped at CY Y-1 and a purge is enforced at split boundaries, but autocorrelation within splits still makes the effective sample size smaller than the row count.

Utilities that merge, change EIA utility number, file multiple state rows, or switch reporting standard are dropped, which removes some large multi-state investor-owned utilities and slightly favours stable filers.

The label multiplies a utility's own baseline by a fixed 1.5 factor, so a utility with an unusually low or unusually volatile three-year baseline is mechanically easier or harder to flag; the rule is frozen before any performance measurement and not re-tuned.

The assumption that a calendar year's final EIA-861 reliability data are public by 31 December of the following year is inferred from observed release timing and the publisher's file listing; freeze exact file vintages and record checksums in a manifest so a later re-release cannot silently change the benchmark.
EIA also publishes early-release versions that exclude utilities pending validation; only final-vintage ZIPs should be used, and the 2025 file should be confirmed final at build time.

Upstream third-party material is excluded: EIA photographs are privately licensed and the EIA logo is a registered trademark that must not be reproduced; only the numeric data are redistributed, and EIA's requested acknowledgment with a publication date must accompany any release.
reason: Form EIA-861's utility-level Reliability schedule is a directly downloadable, non-account, non-PII U.S. federal statistical product published annually since 2013 in one ZIP per calendar year, with the indices (SAIDI/SAIFI/CAIDI, with and without Major Event Days), reporting standard, ownership and customer counts documented by EIA and reproducible against EIA's own published state/national aggregates. It fills a real gap in the existing benchmark (electric distribution reliability operations) and supports a forward, single-source task in which the label uses only the CY Y+1 filing while every input is a CY Y-1-or-earlier filing, so no post-outcome quantity enters the feature vector.

task.decision_user: A state public utility commission reliability analyst or utility distribution-planning manager screening distribution utilities for likely deterioration in routine (non-storm) reliability, to sequence vegetation-management, inspection and hardening review.

task.outcome_horizon: Calendar year Y+1, i.e. the twelve months beginning immediately after the decision instant; the outcome is observed when the CY Y+1 EIA-861 reliability file is published (roughly 9-12 months later).
task.population: U.S. electric distribution utilities identified by EIA utility number that report a non-missing SAIDI excluding major event days in CY Y-3, Y-2 and Y-1 under one consistent reporting standard, report at least 1,000 customers in CY Y-1, carry an ownership code among investor-owned, municipal, cooperative, political subdivision, federal or state, appear with exactly one reliability record in each of those years, and report a SAIDI excluding major event days for CY Y+1. Utilities filing multiple state rows or changing utility number are dropped for that cohort. Missing CY Y+1 outcomes are dropped, never coded negative. No CY Y or later value enters features.
task.prediction_time: 31 December of forecast year Y, using only Form EIA-861 reliability and utility attribute filings for calendar years Y-3, Y-2 and Y-1. Exact historical publication dates are assumed rather than verified. No CY Y or later value enters features.
task.question: Given three years of published distribution-reliability history and utility attributes, will a U.S. electric distribution utility's day-to-day outage duration (SAIDI excluding major event days) jump by at least 50% above its own recent norm in the next calendar year?
task.simple_references: Persistence control: predict 0 for every utility, the minority-class baseline. A lag-level persistence score can be formed from CY Y-1 SAIDI excluding major event days, but it is not a calibrated score for a relative jump. A repeat-last-jump rule predicts 1 when lag1 is at least 1.5 times lag2. Calendar and identity controls are state, ownership-code, reporting-standard and forecast-year base rates fitted on training cohorts only.
task.split_policy: Cohorts are forecast years Y = 2016, 2017, ..., 2024 (labels in CY 2017 ... 2025). Fixed chronological boundaries: train = Y 2016-2019, eval = Y 2020-2021, holdout = Y 2022-2024. No random reassignment and no re-splitting after measurement. Purge rule enforced in code: every feature year is <= Y-1, so the newest training feature year is 2018 while the earliest scored label year is 2021; therefore no training row's feature vector contains a year used to compute any eval or holdout label. Rows whose four-year window (Y-3 ... Y+1) spans a utility-number change or a change of reporting standard are dropped rather than carried across splits.
task.target: Binary y=1 if the utility's reported SAIDI excluding major event days for calendar year Y+1 is greater than or equal to 1.5 times the median of its three reported SAIDI-excluding-major-event-day values for CY Y-3, Y-2 and Y-1; y=0 otherwise. Utilities with a missing CY Y+1 SAIDI-excluding-MED value are dropped, never coded 0.
task.usefulness: The label is not a field in any file. It requires linking four separate annual filings, computing a utility-specific three-year baseline, and observing the next filing. It combines duration with frequency and restoration-speed covariates that a single copied column cannot supply. Deterioration in non-storm reliability is an operational and regulatory screening question that persistence and level-only models handle poorly because the event is a within-utility relative jump rather than a level.

title: Forward prediction of day-to-day distribution reliability deterioration at U.S. electric utilities from Form EIA-861 reliability history
